Find sign combinations that sum to a target

Source: R/find_signs.R
find_signs.Rd

Given a set of labelled values and a target total, determines which multipliers (+1, -1, or 0) to apply to each value so that the signed sum equals the target. Uses a meet-in-the-middle search, so the cost is 2 * 3^(n/2) rather than 3^n.

Usage

find_signs(
  df,
  label_col,
  value_col,
  total_label = "total",
  positive = NULL,
  negative = NULL,
  by = NULL,
  max_zeros = 2L,
  tol = 1e-06
)

Arguments

df

A data frame containing labels and values.

label_col

Column containing item labels, unquoted or as a string.

value_col

Column containing numeric values, unquoted or as a string.

total_label

Label of the row whose value is the reconciliation target. Default: "total".

positive, negative

Labels constrained to a non-negative multiplier (+1, or 0 where max_zeros allows the item to be dropped) or a non-positive one (-1 or 0). Optional. Labels that match nothing are reported.

by

Optional grouping columns: unquoted (by = year), several (by = c(year, firm)), or as strings. The reconciliation is performed separately for each group.

max_zeros

Maximum number of zero coefficients allowed in a solution, i.e. how many items may be excluded. Default: 2L.

tol

Absolute tolerance when comparing a signed sum to the target. Default 1e-6. Filings that round to whole thousands may need more. A tolerance finer than floating point can resolve at the size of the values is raised to that resolution – about 0.001 on a total of a hundred billion.

Value

A tibble with one row per input row, carrying the grouping columns, the label and value columns, and four more: sign (the resolved multiplier, NA when unresolved), certain (whether every candidate agreed on it), n_solutions and status. The value column holds the signed value, or NA where the sign is unresolved.

Details

This reconciles accounting line items whose sign convention is unknown: XBRL amounts often arrive without a meaningful sign, because the convention varies between preparers. An income statement has to add up, and that is enough to recover the signs.

What "solved" means, and what it does not

Uniqueness is not proof. If the true assignment is excluded – say more items than max_zeros genuinely do not belong – a coincidental one can fit alone and be reported as certain. Read a status of "unique" as "only one combination reaches the total", not as "this combination is right".

Nothing is dropped. Every input row comes back, and status says what happened to its group:

  • "unique" – exactly one assignment reaches the total.

  • "ambiguous" – several do. Items that get the same sign in all of them are still determined, so their sign is filled in with certain = TRUE; the rest are NA. This is a logical consequence, not a guess.

  • "unsolved" – no assignment reaches the total within max_zeros.

  • "no_total" / "duplicate_total" – the group has no row labelled total_label, or more than one.

Among competing assignments, those using the fewest zeros are preferred: a solution that uses every reported line item is more plausible than one that discards two. status and n_solutions describe the group after that preference is applied.

Why a search, and not the taxonomy's weights

XBRL has a place for these weights: the calculation linkbase. The Danish taxonomy does not fill it. Across its 13 versions from 2010 to 2025 the one calculation linkbase is a 2020 income statement for one kind of education institution, so for an ordinary annual report the arithmetic is the only route to a sign. The taxonomy does mark every line debit or credit. Over 8,633 income statement lines solved in a 4,304-filing corpus and reported positive, the sign found here agrees with that marking for 99.8%, and the rest are elements whose direction varies by nature, such as changes in inventories.

See also

read_xbrl(), and check_cascade(), which uses the debit/credit marking to break ties.

Examples

items <- data.frame(
  label = c("revenue", "costs", "depreciation", "total"),
  value = c(100, 40, 10, 50)
)
find_signs(items, label, value, total_label = "total")
#> # A tibble: 4 × 6
#>   label        value  sign certain n_solutions status
#>   <chr>        <dbl> <int> <lgl>         <int> <chr> 
#> 1 revenue        100     1 TRUE              1 unique
#> 2 costs          -40    -1 TRUE              1 unique
#> 3 depreciation   -10    -1 TRUE              1 unique
#> 4 total           50     1 TRUE              1 unique
